title: Week 1 quiz: Capabilities and how they are measured

questions.prompt: What quantity did the Kaplan (2020) and Chinchilla (2022) scaling laws model as a power law in compute, parameters, and data?

options.text: Accuracy on downstream benchmarks such as MMLU
options.rationale: Benchmark accuracy is bounded and often S-shaped; the laws were fit to loss.

options.text: Pretraining test loss (next-token cross-entropy) on held-out text
options.rationale: Yes. Both papers fit loss, which is why claims about tasks are extrapolations from them.

options.text: The number of tasks a model can complete autonomously
options.rationale: That is closer to METR's time-horizon measure, introduced in 2025.

options.text: User preference votes
options.rationale: That is what arena leaderboards measure.

questions.explanation: Scaling laws are among the most reliable empirical results in the field, for the quantity they measure. The mapping from lower loss to useful capability is a separate, weaker empirical relationship, and most public arguments about timelines quietly assume it.

questions.prompt: Using the rule of thumb that training compute is about 6 times parameters times tokens, what does this print?
questions.code:
N = 8e9        # parameters
D = 15e12      # training tokens
C = 6 * N * D
print(f"{C:.1e}", round(D / N))

options.rationale: 6 times 8e9 times 15e12 is 7.2e23; 15e12 divided by 8e9 is 1,875 tokens per parameter.
That forgets the factor of 6 and assumes the Chinchilla ratio rather than computing it.
The compute is right, but the tokens-per-parameter ratio is computed from the given numbers, not assumed.
Check the multiplication: 8 times 15 is 120, times 6 is 720.

questions.explanation: At about 1,900 tokens per parameter, this model is trained far past the Chinchilla ratio of about 20. That is deliberate in many open-weight releases: extra training compute buys a smaller model that is cheaper to serve. Compute-optimal for training is not optimal for deployment.

questions.prompt: Which are documented drivers of capability gains from 2024 to 2026, according to this week's primary sources? Select all that apply.

options.text: Reinforcement learning on tasks with checkable answers, such as math and code
options.rationale: The o1 announcement (September 2024) and the DeepSeek-R1 paper (January 2025) both describe this.

options.text: More test-time compute: letting models generate more intermediate reasoning before answering
options.rationale: The International AI Safety Report 2026 calls this inference-time scaling and credits it with large gains on complex reasoning.

options.text: Continued scaling of initial training compute
options.rationale: The same report notes that more initial training compute still improves models, even as post-training gains grow.

options.text: The discovery that loss no longer matters for capability
options.rationale: No source claims this.

questions.explanation: The scaling story now has several axes with different cost curves. When someone says scaling is over or accelerating, ask which axis they mean.

questions.prompt: A board member shows you a chart of a capability metric that has risen in a straight line on a log scale for six years and says, "So by 2028 it will be 100 times higher." What is the most useful response?

options.text: Agree; log-linear trends in AI have been very stable.
options.rationale: Stable so far is evidence, not a guarantee, and it says nothing about what the metric measures.

options.text: Disagree; exponential trends always end.
options.rationale: True eventually, but it does not tell you when, so it is not a useful forecast either.

options.text: Ask what the metric measures and where its measurement ceiling is, show how the 2028 figure changes under a slower doubling time, and name the evidence that would confirm or break the trend.
options.rationale: Yes. That turns a single extrapolation into a range with explicit assumptions.

questions.explanation: The METR horizon is a good example: the trend was steady, the measurement suite ran out of long tasks in 2026, and the implied dates move by years with reasonable changes in doubling time or reliability level.

questions.prompt: Why did OpenAI stop reporting SWE-bench Verified scores in February 2026?

options.text: Its models scored too low to be competitive.
options.rationale: The issue was the benchmark's validity, not OpenAI's scores.

options.text: An audit found many remaining problems had flawed tests or descriptions, and gains increasingly reflected exposure to the benchmark during training.
options.rationale: Yes. Of 138 audited problems, 59.4% had material flaws; OpenAI recommended SWE-bench Pro instead.

options.text: The benchmark's maintainers withdrew it.
options.rationale: The decision described in this week's source was OpenAI's own.

options.text: Regulators banned public coding benchmarks.
options.rationale: No such regulation exists.

questions.explanation: This is the full life cycle of a benchmark: introduced, trusted, saturated and contaminated, audited, replaced. When you see a score, ask where in that cycle the benchmark sits.

questions.prompt: This code is meant to report a model's improvement on a benchmark. What is the main problem with the conclusion it prints?
questions.code:
old = [1]*412 + [0]*88   # 500 items, 82.4%
new = [1]*421 + [0]*79   # 500 items, 84.2%
delta = sum(new)/500 - sum(old)/500
print(f"New model is better by {delta:.1%}")

options.text: It reports a 1.8-point difference with no interval, no paired comparison by item, and no check for run-to-run variance, so it may be noise.
options.rationale: Yes. Benchmark variance studies (Madaan and colleagues, 2024) show differences this size can flip between runs.

options.text: The arithmetic is wrong; the difference is 9 points.
options.rationale: 9 is the difference in counts; divided by 500 it is 1.8 points.

options.text: 500 items is too many to compare.
options.rationale: More items help; the problem is the missing uncertainty estimate.

questions.explanation: With 500 items near 83%, the standard error of each rate is about 1.7 points, and of an unpaired difference about 2.4 points. A paired analysis by item can do better, but you have to run it. Report n, an interval, and the comparison method before concluding.

questions.prompt: Which statement about METR's time-horizon measurements in 2026 is accurate?

options.text: They show frontier agents reliably completing month-long tasks.
options.rationale: Public 80% horizons were about 1.5 hours in early 2026.

options.text: METR warned that measurements above about 16 hours are unreliable with its current task suite, and stopped actively updating its public page in September 2026.
options.rationale: Yes. The ruler ran out of length during 2026.

options.text: The doubling time slowed to about two years under Time Horizon 1.1.
options.rationale: TH1.1 found a faster post-2023 doubling time, about 131 days.

options.text: They cover all professional domains equally.
options.rationale: The suite is mostly software, ML, and cybersecurity.

questions.explanation: Good measurement organizations publish the limits of their instruments. Quote them alongside the numbers.

questions.prompt: You must choose a model for transcribing and summarizing hour-long customer-call recordings (audio) into structured notes, at about 2,000 calls a day. Which plan is best supported by this week's lessons?

options.text: Pick whichever model is first on the Arena text leaderboard.
options.rationale: Text preference rankings say little about audio input, structured output, or cost at volume.

options.text: Shortlist models whose providers document native audio input (for example Gemini 4 models) plus a pipeline of a speech-to-text model feeding a cheaper text model; evaluate both on 30 labeled calls for field accuracy, cost per call, and latency; pick the cheapest that clears the bar on its lower confidence bound.
options.rationale: Yes. Documented features set the shortlist; a small eval on your data decides.

options.text: Use the most expensive flagship available, because quality matters most.
options.rationale: At 2,000 calls a day, cost differences of 10x to 100x matter, and a cheaper option may clear the bar.

questions.explanation: Modality is a hard constraint that filters the shortlist before capability does. Then the usual eval applies: real inputs, a written rubric, a cheaper alternative in the comparison, and a decision on lower bounds.

questions.prompt: What does this print? (It computes the lower end of a 95% Wilson interval.)
questions.code:
import math
def wilson_lower(k, n, z=1.96):
    p = k / n
    d = 1 + z*z/n
    c = p + z*z/(2*n)
    m = z * math.sqrt(p*(1-p)/n + z*z/(4*n*n))
    return (c - m) / d
print(round(wilson_lower(19, 20), 2), round(wilson_lower(95, 100), 2))

options.rationale: Same 95% pass rate, but with 20 items the plausible floor is 76%; with 100 items it is 89%.
Those are the point estimates, not the lower bounds.
Reversed: more data gives a tighter interval and a higher lower bound.

questions.explanation: Decide model choices on lower bounds, and buy more eval items when a cheap model's lower bound sits just under your bar. Sample size is part of the evidence.

questions.prompt: Which of these are documented biases or caveats of arena-style leaderboards? Select all that apply.

options.text: Answer length and formatting influence votes.
options.rationale: The Arena team's own style-control analysis found this.

options.text: Some providers privately tested many variants and could choose which to publish.
options.rationale: Reported in "The Leaderboard Illusion" (Singh and colleagues, 2025).

options.text: Votes measure preference, which is not the same as correctness.
options.rationale: A confident wrong answer can win a vote.

options.text: Votes are cast by the model providers themselves.
options.rationale: Votes come from users; the concern is how providers can shape what gets ranked.

questions.explanation: Arena rankings are a useful signal of what people prefer on their own prompts. Use them to shortlist, and remember what they cannot tell you.
